newsitem.title: DUBAI: UAE's Etisalat expects new satellite by end 2000.
newsitem.headline: UAE's Etisalat expects new satellite by end 2000.

text.p: Etisalat, the United Arab Emirates telecommunications giant, expects to complete a multi-million satellite project for mobile communications by turn of the century, the official news agency WAM said on Tuesday.
The decision was taken during an Etisalat board meeting chaired by Minister of State for Finance and Industrial Affairs Ahmed bin Humaid al-Tayer -- acting Communications Minister.

Etisalat director-general Ali Oweiss told WAM the new company, al-Thurayya for Satellite Communications, would have a starting capital of $25 million to be increased to $500 million within six months.
"The final decision will be taken in the next three months...and we expect to execute the Thurayya project before the end of the year 2000," Oweiss added.
Total costs for the project would be around $800 million and it was expected to post 20 percent in annual profits, he said.
The system will provide services to UAE users of two-way mobile telephones compatible with the Global System for Mobile Communications (GSM).
It will make services available to remote sea and rural areas amd will cover most Arab states, parts of the Indian subcontinent, Central Asia, North Africa and parts of Europe.
Etisalat board agreed to hand out a memo detailing all information on the project to help form a UAE-based shareholding company, WAM said.
Etisalat will hold 26 percent of Thurayya's shares while 51 percent will go to UAE nationals and leading local investment and financial firms, it added.
Arab Satellite Communications Organisation (Arabsat) and other regional telecommunications departments will be offered the rest.
Arabsat, which operates satellite communications for Arab countries including television, telephone and data transmission, is jointly owned by 21 Arab states.
Oweiss said the board reviewed three offers from two French and an American, all giant manufacturers. He did not name them.

"One of them made an offer that was $50 million less than what was expected, but the three offers have been referred to a German consultant to see how close they match with requested specifications," he said.
Etisalat in July invited European and North American firms to bid for the deal and gave them three months to make the offer in a highly competitive market.
Industry sources then identified them as France's Alcatel, Aerospatiale and U.S. Hughes Electronics Corp.
